explanations.explanation: True, baker. The LORD’s words name “…oxen and sheep, camels and donkeys.” The animals are in the command right alongside the people. It's a heavy command, and the story doesn't hurry past it. Keep those animals in mind, because they come back.

Not this time, friend. Listen to how the LORD puts it: “…oxen and sheep, camels and donkeys.” The animals are named right there next to the people. Hold on to that, because the animals don't stay in the background for long.

explanations.answer: They were kind to Israel leaving Egypt
explanations.explanation: Kindness, friend. Saul tells the Kenites, “Since you showed kindness to all the Israelites when they came up out of Egypt, go on and get away from the Amalekites.” That kindness got them a warning and a way out. It's a good reminder that a kind thing you did can still be remembered later.

explanations.answer: They paid Saul to protect them
explanations.explanation: Nobody slides Saul an envelope in this scene. Payment never comes up. The reason Saul gives is kindness: “Since you showed kindness to all the Israelites when they came up out of Egypt…” The Kenites got their warning for what they had already done.

explanations.answer: They promised to fight for Saul
explanations.explanation: Not a word about the Kenites promising to fight. Saul gives them their reason himself: “Since you showed kindness to all the Israelites…” The warning rests on something they had already done, not on a promise. I'd say that's a kindness being remembered.

I get why that seems possible, friend, but the text says otherwise. After Saul's warning, “…the Kenites moved away from the Amalekites.” No arguing, no lingering. When someone says get out or get swept away, you pack the cart.

That's right, the Kenites listen. Verse 6 ends with “So the Kenites moved away from the Amalekites.” Saul warned them once and they took it. I wish I'd moved that fast the first time somebody told me to get out of the dough.
Agag it is, baker. The text says Saul “…captured Agag king of Amalek alive…” Hang on to that name. A king captured alive is a detail you don't want to lose track of.

Achish is a real name in the Bible, but he was king of Gath (1 Samuel 21:10), not king of the Amalekites. Saul captures Agag alive. Different king, different city, friend. Easy to mix up when the names are stacked this close together.

Eglon was king of Moab (Judges 3:12), which is another nation altogether. The Amalekite king Saul captures alive is Agag. I mix up names all the time too. Ask me which cutter is Berry and which is Buttercup and I'd get it right, but ask me on a bad day and who knows.

Best, friend. Saul and his troops spared “…the best of the sheep and cattle, the fat calves and lambs, and the best of everything else.” Nobody picks out the weakest ones first. I've never once reached for the burnt cookie first, so I understand the pull.

Nobody keeps the weakest, baker. I'm the stamper who grabs the best-looking cookie off the cooling rack, and the troops did that with the livestock. The text says they spared “…the best of the sheep and cattle…” It's the opposite of weakest.
Age isn't what the text points to. It says they spared “…the best of the sheep and cattle, the fat calves and lambs…” Calves and lambs are young, so oldest doesn't fit. What they kept was the best.

That's the one. The text says “…they devoted to destruction all that was despised and worthless.” It's like keeping the pretty cookies for yourself and sending the crumbs to the oven. And in this verse, the best is what they were unwilling to devote.
Not every animal, friend. Verse 9 says they spared “…the best of the sheep and cattle…” They were unwilling to devote those. What they devoted was “…all that was despised and worthless.”

The text never says whose things these were. It says they spared Agag himself, along with the best, and “…they devoted to destruction all that was despised and worthless.” So the line they drew was between best and worthless, not between owners. That's the part to remember.

Regrets. The LORD says, “I regret that I have made Saul king, for he has turned away from following Me and has not carried out My instructions.” That's a hard line to read. The LORD gives the reason right there in the verse.
Not here, baker. The LORD says, “I regret that I have made Saul king…” That's the word, regret. It's a heavy moment, so there's no joke in this one.

There's no rejoicing in this verse, friend. The LORD says, “I regret that I have made Saul king, for he has turned away from following Me and has not carried out My instructions.” No confetti, no cookies. It's a sad word from the LORD, and it's meant to be heard that way.

explanations.answer: Cries out to the LORD all night
explanations.explanation: Samuel was distressed, and he “…cried out to the LORD all that night.” He doesn't call a meeting or fire off a message. He takes the whole thing to the LORD. I think that tells you how much it hit him.

explanations.answer: Calls the elders together that night
explanations.explanation: The text never has Samuel calling the elders. It says Samuel “…was distressed and cried out to the LORD all that night.” His night goes to the LORD, not to a meeting. No elders, no agenda, just a prophet who is hurting.

explanations.answer: Writes Saul a warning that night
explanations.explanation: No letter in this scene, friend. Samuel's night is spent like this: “…Samuel was distressed and cried out to the LORD all that night.” The talking with Saul comes in the morning, face to face. The night belongs to the LORD.

That's it, baker. Samuel is told that Saul “…has set up a monument for himself and has turned and gone down to Gilgal.” Samuel hears it secondhand, from whoever told him. Me, I've got my name carved on my handle by the Millers, and I'd never ask for a monument on top of it.
The report says nothing about an altar. It says Saul “…has set up a monument for himself…” That's a monument with Saul's name on the idea, friend. An altar would have been a different story.
No camp in the report, baker. What Samuel is told is that Saul “…has set up a monument for himself…” The troops aren't mentioned in that sentence. It's all about Saul.
True, friend. Saul says, “May the LORD bless you. I have carried out the LORD’s instructions.” He says it in the same breath as the greeting. Samuel hasn't asked a single question yet.

It's actually true, baker, so this one flips. Saul says, “May the LORD bless you. I have carried out the LORD’s instructions.” The blessing and the report come in one breath. Samuel hasn't asked him anything yet.

Sheep and cattle, baker. Samuel asks, “Then what is this bleating of sheep and lowing of cattle that I hear?” Saul had just said the job was done, and the animals didn't get the memo. Sheep are terrible at keeping secrets.
No trumpets in this scene, friend. Samuel asks about “…this bleating of sheep and lowing of cattle that I hear?” His ear is on the animals. Nobody had to blow a horn to give Saul away.

No cheering here, baker. The sound Samuel asks about is “…bleating of sheep and lowing of cattle…” It's a quiet question with a loud answer standing right there in the camp. Samuel doesn't need a crowd to hear it.
The troops, friend. Saul answers, “The troops brought them from the Amalekites…” When one of my batches burns, I blame the oven. Saul reaches for the troops.

The Kenites already moved away from the Amalekites back in verse 6, so they're not the ones Saul names here. He says, “The troops brought them from the Amalekites…” That's who he points to. The Kenites are out of this scene.
The elders aren't in this scene, baker. Saul says, “The troops brought them from the Amalekites…” That's his answer to the sound of the animals. He names the troops, not any elders.
That's Saul's answer. He says they spared the best sheep and cattle “…to sacrifice to the LORD your God…” It sounds holy, friend. But Samuel isn't done talking yet.
Saul never says that, baker. He says the best were spared “…to sacrifice to the LORD your God…” Feeding the troops isn't in his answer. I'd have loved to see a snack plan, but he doesn't give one.
Saul doesn't mention giving anything to the elders. What he says is that the best were spared “…to sacrifice to the LORD your God…” That's his whole reason. The elders aren't in it.

Plunder, baker. Samuel asks, “So why did you not obey the LORD? Why did you rush upon the plunder and do evil in the sight of the LORD?” Plunder is what's taken from a defeated enemy. Rush upon is a strong phrase, and Samuel chose it.

The Philistines aren't in Samuel's question, friend. He asks about rushing upon “…the plunder…” and doing evil in the sight of the LORD. This battle was with the Amalekites. Easy to grab a name that sounds like it fits.

Samuel isn't talking about prophets, baker. He asks, “Why did you rush upon the plunder and do evil in the sight of the LORD?” The word he uses is plunder. Rushing at the prophets would be a whole different chapter.

I'd have guessed that too, friend, but Saul doesn't give in. He says, “But I did obey the LORD.” He says he went on the mission and brought back Agag. The words “I have sinned” don't come until later.
False is right, baker. Saul answers Samuel with “But I did obey the LORD,” and he says he went on the mission and brought back Agag king of Amalek. No admission yet. That comes later in the chapter.

That's it. Samuel says, “Behold, obedience is better than sacrifice, and attentiveness is better than the fat of rams.” Saul kept pointing at sacrifices, and Samuel points at listening. A full cookie box doesn't beat doing what you were asked.

More animals isn't what Samuel says. He says, “Behold, obedience is better than sacrifice, and attentiveness is better than the fat of rams.” Piling on more doesn't fix it, friend. He points to obedience.

A bigger altar isn't in Samuel's answer, baker. He says, “…obedience is better than sacrifice, and attentiveness is better than the fat of rams.” What he points to is obeying and paying attention. No construction needed.

Rejected him as king, baker. Samuel says, “Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, He has rejected you as king.” That's a big line. Saul pushed aside the word of the LORD, and Samuel tells him where it leaves him.
Samuel doesn't say anything about the army, friend. He says, “Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, He has rejected you as king.” The word is king, not army. That's the weight of the verse.
No sickness in this verse, baker. Samuel says, “Because you have rejected the word of the LORD, He has rejected you as king.” That's the whole message. It's about the kingship.

explanations.answer: He feared the people and obeyed them
explanations.explanation: That's his reason, friend. Saul says, “I have sinned; I have transgressed the LORD’s commandment and your instructions, because I feared the people and obeyed their voice.” He says it plainly. That's a real thing to say out loud.
Saul doesn't say he forgot, baker. He says he has transgressed “…because I feared the people and obeyed their voice.” That's the reason he gives. Forgetting never comes up.

explanations.answer: Agag offered him a peace treaty
explanations.explanation: No peace treaty in the text, friend. Saul's reason is, “…because I feared the people and obeyed their voice.” Agag doesn't speak in this scene at all. It's the people Saul points to.

explanations.answer: To forgive him and come back with him
explanations.explanation: That's what he asks. Saul says, “Now therefore, please forgive my sin and return with me so I can worship the LORD.” He asks for forgiveness and for company. I think it's a lot to put in one sentence.

explanations.answer: To anoint him king a second time
explanations.explanation: Saul doesn't ask for a second anointing, baker. He asks, “Now therefore, please forgive my sin and return with me so I can worship the LORD.” Forgiveness and a walk back with him. That's the whole request.

explanations.answer: To pray for the troops at Gilgal
explanations.explanation: The troops aren't part of the request, friend. Saul says, “…please forgive my sin and return with me so I can worship the LORD.” He wants forgiveness and he wants Samuel to return with him. No prayer list.

I see why you'd hope so, baker, but Samuel says no. His words are, “I will not return with you.” He adds that Saul has rejected the word of the LORD, and the LORD has rejected him as king over Israel. That's a firm no.

False, friend. Samuel answers, “I will not return with you. For you have rejected the word of the LORD, and He has rejected you as king over Israel.” That first answer is a no. It's a hard moment, and Samuel doesn't soften it.
It tears. Saul grabbed the hem of Samuel's robe, “…and it tore.” One grab, one rip. And Samuel is about to say something about it.
It doesn't slip, baker. The text says Saul grabbed the hem “…and it tore.” A slip I could laugh at. A tear is a bigger deal.
Stretching would just be a laundry problem, friend. The text says the hem of the robe “…tore.” That word matters for what Samuel says next. Don't let it slip past.
The kingdom, baker. Samuel says, “The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today…” Notice he uses the same word as the robe. The torn hem and the torn kingdom go together in his words.
The army's loyalty isn't what Samuel names, friend. He says, “The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today…” It's the kingdom. Nothing about the troops.
Samuel doesn't mention Saul's family in that line, baker. He says, “The LORD has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today…” It's the kingdom that's torn away. That's the whole sentence.
Neighbor, friend. Samuel says the LORD “…has given it to your neighbor who is better than you.” He doesn't name him here. I'd say that's a mystery worth keeping.
Samuel doesn't say son, baker. He says the LORD “…has given it to your neighbor who is better than you.” So it goes outside Saul's own household. He doesn't give a name in this verse.
Brother isn't in the verse, friend. Samuel says it has been given “…to your neighbor who is better than you.” That's who he points to, without a name. I'd keep an eye out for who it is.
Honor, baker. Saul says, “Please honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel.” He wants it done in front of them. I think that stands out after what he just heard.
Crown isn't what Saul asks for. He says, “Please honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel.” The word is honor, friend. He asks for it in front of the elders and all Israel.
Defend isn't in the request, baker. Saul says, “Please honor me now before the elders of my people and before Israel.” He's asking for honor, out in the open. That's the word he picks.
True, friend. The text says, “So Samuel went back with Saul, and Saul worshiped the LORD.” The first time Samuel said no. This time Samuel goes back with him.

False was the answer for the first ask, baker, but not this one. The text says, “So Samuel went back with Saul, and Saul worshiped the LORD.” This time Samuel goes. Same question twice, different answer.

explanations.answer: The danger of death is behind him
explanations.explanation: That's what Agag thinks. The text says, “Surely the bitterness of death is past.” He walks up cheerfully, friend, and he's sure of it. This part is heavy.

explanations.answer: Samuel wants to make peace with Amalek
explanations.explanation: Peace isn't what the text gives as Agag's thought. It says, “Surely the bitterness of death is past.” That's the whole thought. It's a heavy moment, friend.

explanations.answer: He is about to get his throne back
explanations.explanation: A throne isn't in Agag's thought, baker. The text gives it as, “Surely the bitterness of death is past.” That's what he thinks as he walks up cheerfully. It's a heavy scene, so I'll leave it there.
Gibeah, baker. The text says Samuel went to Ramah, “…but Saul went up to his home in Gibeah of Saul.” Two men, two roads home. They're heading in different directions.
Mizpah isn't where the verse sends him, friend. It says, “…Saul went up to his home in Gibeah of Saul.” Samuel goes to Ramah. Neither of them goes to Mizpah.
Bethel isn't in this verse, baker. The text says Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul “…went up to his home in Gibeah of Saul.” Home for Saul is Gibeah. I'd keep that name handy.
I understand the hope, baker, but the text says no. “…Samuel never again visited Saul.” It adds that he kept that up to the day of Saul's death. This line is heavy.

False, friend. The text says, “…Samuel never again visited Saul. Samuel mourned for Saul…” He stayed away to the day of Saul's death, and he mourned for him. That's a sad ending to this part of the story.
